articles.title: Correcting measurement error bias in conjoint survey experiments
articles.authors: Katherine Clayton, Yusaku Horiuchi, Aaron R. Kaufman, Gary King, Mayya Komisarchik
articles.abstract: Conjoint survey designs are spreading across the social sciences due to their unusual capacity to estimate many causal effects from a single randomized experiment. Unfortunately, by their ability to mirror complicated real‐world choices, these designs often generate substantial measurement error and thus bias. We replicate both the data collection and analysis from eight prominent conjoint studies, all of which closely reproduce published results, and reveal high levels of measurement error in all. We then discover a common empirical pattern in how measurement error appears in conjoint studies and, with it, introduce an easy‐to‐use statistical method to correct the bias. Along the way, we provide a much simpler and simultaneously more powerful approach to designing, organizing, understanding, and analyzing conjoint data analyses.

articles.title: Contested Governance and Civilian Prosocial Behavior: Evidence from Lab-in-the-Field Experiments in India
articles.authors: BRANDON BOLTE, VINEETA YADAV, BUMBA MUKHERJEE
articles.abstract: How does contested governance by states and competing armed actors affect the behavior of the governed? During civil conflicts, rebel organizations frequently provide public goods, judicial arbitration, and security, but these forms of governance often operate alongside local state institutions. Beyond avoiding violence, therefore, noncombatants must navigate the daily uncertainty of local governance by states and armed groups vying for territorial control. This, we argue, shapes their quotidian interactions with one another. Using a series of lab-in-the-field experiments and surveys from Naxal-affected Bihar, India, we find that individuals living under such contested governance exhibit greater interpersonal trust and trustworthiness and less opportunistic behavior. We propose two mechanisms to explain these patterns—fearing intra-community retaliation or substituting for the state with interpersonal reliance. Most evidence is only consistent with the latter. By connecting governance, rebellion, and social capital, this work makes important contributions toward understanding the micro-politics of local order during longstanding armed conflicts.

articles.title: Still Instrumentally Inclusive
articles.authors: STUART J. TURNBULL-DUGARTE, ALBERTO LÓPEZ ORTEGA
articles.abstract: Do individuals in Western democracies shift their views on LGBT+ inclusion when exposed to opposition from Muslim out-groups? And is this “homonationalist” responsiveness stronger among anti-immigration individuals? Our article “Instrumentally inclusive […]” addressed these questions using representative data from Britain (Study 1) and crowd-sourced data from Spain (Study 2). We revisit Study 2 in response to concerns about post-stratification weighting a convenience sample and erroneously inconsistent use of robust standard errors. Varying population reference parameters, weight caps, variance estimators, subgroup definitions, and covariate adjustments, we find strong support for the original findings. Neither reasonable alternative weighting schemes nor corrected variance estimators substantively change the results. In fact, the originally published point estimates are equal to or smaller than the median across alternative specifications. Consistent with the Article, we find that treatment increases support for LGBT+ inclusion in Spain, without consistent identifiable variation by immigration attitudes.

articles.title: Is Blood Thicker Than Water(-and-Earth)? Partisanship Geography in Imperial China and the Limits of Quantitative History
articles.abstract: Using Wang Anshi’s Reform as a case study, Yuhua Wang’s “Blood is Thicker Than Water” ( American Political Science Review , 2022) argues that geographically dispersed kinship networks incentivize political elites to support the building of a strong state, whereas geographically concentrated kinship networks undermine state building. In this article, I improve the sample with the help of additional historical records and show that the reported correlation fails to replicate when either the control issue or the outlier issue is considered. I then propose two alternative hypotheses on the role of kinship network dispersal in Wang Anshi’s Reform, based on two common explanations of its partisanship geography in Chinese historical scholarship, that is, status competition and policy adaptiveness. After examining those hypotheses respectively, I reflect on the limits of quantitative history that this case illustrates.

articles.title: Thinly Veiled: The Use of Femonationalist Speech in European Parliaments
articles.authors: Jorge M. Fernandes, Bonnie M. Meguid, Ana Catalano Weeks
articles.abstract: Femonationalism – the use of gendered rhetoric to promote nativist anti-immigration views – is thought to be on the rise across Western European democracies, but scholars lack a systematic understanding of its prevalence across parties and countries, the conditions under which it appears, and the role gender plays in its use. To make progress on these questions, this study explores the use of femonationalism in legislative speeches from five Western European countries from 2009 to 2024. Combining dictionary methods with topic modeling, we find that far-right parties are most likely to use femonationalist rhetoric, increasing these appeals when party opponents threaten their issue distinctiveness by converging towards their anti-immigration policy position. Crucially, our analysis also highlights the role of gender in shaping femonationalist rhetoric: while the overall strategy is party-driven, men and women legislators emphasize different dimensions of femonationalism, with men focusing on security concerns and women invoking gender equality.

articles.title: The Equality Positions and Policies of Governments, 1970–2020: How Egalitarian Parties Evoke Equality While Evading Real Redistribution
articles.abstract: Despite egalitarian rhetoric, governments often fail to implement redistributive policies. We argue that selective egalitarianism helps to understand this puzzle. Analysing a new dataset of 850,000 manifesto statements and equality policies in 12 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries (1970–2020), we show that even parties committed to equality avoid taxing the rich. Instead of engaging in complex top-end taxation, which is perceived as electorally risky, they pursue pre-distribution and welfare policies with less concentrated costs and complexity. Even these policies are primarily adopted if the party’s constituency is not too educated or rich to benefit from them. Our findings suggest that equality-oriented governments adopt an approach that insures the middle, buffers the poor, but spares the rich. The result is a rhetorical commitment to equality that eschews its most redistributive instrument(s). The patterns we reveal help to explain the consequential disconnect between redistributive demand and actual policy, even under ostensibly economically egalitarian governments.

articles.title: Disproportionality in Geographic Representation
articles.authors: Orit Kedar, Yair Amitai, Gilad Hurvitz
articles.abstract: We theoretically develop and empirically study the concept of geographic representation. We identify an overlooked aspect of (mis)representation in electoral systems: the degree to which within parties, voters residing in some districts are overrepresented at the expense of their co-partisans residing elsewhere. Drawing on district-level data of 113 parties from twelve districted democracies, we find a substantial degree of geographic representational discrepancies within parties. Importantly, we show that the discrepancy is often accompanied by a difference in policy positions between under and overrepresented districts, making it particularly significant politically. We derive a general measure for the discrepancy between the votes a party gains and the seats it holds in different districts, namely, geographic disproportionality (GeoDisp). Unlike malapportionment, GeoDisp is party specific and draws on actual votes. Utilizing geocoded data, we find a substantial degree of geographic disproportionality, which, per our expectations, varies systematically by party.

articles.title: Exodus and vote: Mass emigration and voter turnout in Honduras
Who won the feed? TikTok campaigning of the alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left in Germany’s 2025 federal election
Beyond the ideal type: Investigating ‘mixed preferences’ for who should govern in nine European countries
articles.authors: Sebastien Rojon, Jean-Benoit Pilet, Paulina Pankowska, Davide Vittori, Emilien Paulis
articles.abstract: Noting widespread disenchantment with representative actors and institutions, a growing field of research has investigated public support for decision-making by alternative actors, such as ordinary citizens and independent experts. However, previous research has mainly focused on ideal-type models of government centred on a single actor, rather than considering that citizens may hold ‘mixed preferences’ for multiple actors. Through a latent profile analysis of survey responses to an established battery measuring preferences for who should govern, we identify six preference types that exist across nine European countries, though their prevalence varies from country to country. The results show that only a small minority of respondents support an ideal-type model, i.e., the representative democrats, while most favour a combination of actors. A sizeable share of respondents continues to support politicians but would like to see greater involvement from either citizens or experts. Finally, we identify three profiles that lack strong theoretical or empirical grounding in previous research but emerge across multiple countries and therefore merit further attention: stealth populists, responsible democrats, and moderates.

articles.title: When the party is over: How parties respond to electoral decline
articles.abstract: Over the past decades, we have witnessed the severe electoral decline of formerly successful parties. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how these parties have responded to their losses. I examine the consequences of severe and persistent electoral losses through the lens of intra-party dynamics. I argue that parties react to severe decline by shifting attention to core issues and adopting more extreme positions. I theorize that this is because office-seekers are the first to abandon the sinking ship, tilting the internal power balance towards policy-motivated actors. Testing the theory with manifesto data from 18 Western European countries between 1970 and 2025, I find evidence that parties devote more attention to their core issues following their electoral decline. Parties do not, however, adopt more extreme positions on these issues. I find limited evidence that shifts in the intra-party balance are behind these changes.

articles.title: Allocative claims and pork barrel politics
articles.authors: Marius Sältzer, Hauke Peters, Charlotte Keyßler
articles.abstract: Political strategies are shaped by electoral institutions and incentives. There is a large literature on pork barrel politics in single-member districts (SMD), but understanding the institutional effects that shape the incentives for pork requires comparison within the same system. The German Mixed-Member Electoral system offers an ideal institutional setup, but official data on pork is not available. Instead, we focus on the use of pork references as an electoral strategy, adapting credit-claiming theory to textual analysis of candidates’ social media posts. Using supervised machine learning on Facebook posts by candidates in the 2017 and 2021 federal election campaign period, we fine-tune a BERT classifier on 1000 manually coded posts to identify pork references (F1: 0.82). Our results demonstrate that incumbents, particularly district incumbents and those who outperform their national party’s vote share, are significantly more likely to emphasize pork in their communication. Moreover, candidates are more likely to use pork references if their competitors within the district employ similar strategies, and when electoral competition in the district is high. Our findings imply that particularistic logic exists beyond SMDs and can be shaped by the internal specificities of more complex incentive systems.

articles.title: Party responsiveness to party supporters, the electorate, and interest groups in a multidimensional policy space
articles.abstract: This article sheds new light on party responsiveness by considering the role of interest group pressure in parties’ responsiveness to their supporters and the electorate on multiple policy dimensions in 12 countries. Following recent work, we expect that parties are as responsive to shifts in their supporters’ preferences as to the wider electorate. Yet, parties also attend to interest group pressure. We argue that parties’ responsiveness to voters is enhanced by leadership ties with interest groups but that ties with only sectional groups are associated with more stable party positions. Combining data on voters, interest groups, and parties, our analysis shows that parties are responsive to preference change among their supporters and, further, that their policy positions are more stable when they only have ties with sectional groups. However, parties’ responsiveness on specific dimensions is not necessarily enhanced by leadership ties with the interest groups particularly active on those dimensions.

articles.title: Technocracy or not, this is the question: can party system predict the number of technocrats in governments?
articles.abstract: In the last three decades, Europe has witnessed an increase in the number of technocrats – non-partisan, non-elected experts appointed on the basis of technical competence – in government. This paper examines whether structural characteristics of party systems predict the share of technocrats in cabinets across 30 European countries between 2000 and 2024. Building on theories of party competition, delegation, and representation, it investigates how systemic features of party democracy shape technocratic appointments. Using fractional regression models, the study tests the relationship between the share of technocrats and three key party-system variables: ideological polarization, party system fragmentation, and party institutionalization. The findings reveal that technocrats are significantly more prevalent where ideological distance between parties complicates bargaining and creates demand for neutral mediators who can bridge incompatible policy positions. Conversely, when more parties compete for portfolios, partisan actors crowd out non-partisan experts rather than delegating to them. Most importantly, in systems where parties possess stable organizations, coherent programmatic profiles, and deep societal roots, technocratic inclusion is significantly lower.

articles.title: More than a partisan pandemic: Worldview and COVID ‐19 response in the United States
articles.authors: Marc J. Hetherington, Andrew M. Engelhardt, Isaac D. Mehlhaff
articles.abstract: As the COVID‐19 pandemic unfolded, public responses increasingly divided along political lines: Democrats tended to support policies and behaviors recommended by public health experts and Republicans tended to oppose them. We argue that exclusively party‐based explanations for these patterns are incomplete. Instead, we call attention to people's philosophy about life—their “worldview”—as an important force behind their pandemic responses. We posit that citizens use beliefs derived from interactions with their everyday life to inform their affinities and preferences when analogous matters enter the political realm. Using original cross‐sectional and panel survey data gathered over the course of the pandemic, we theorize and empirically validate a multidimensional measure of worldview. We show that worldview is a coherent, belief‐system‐like entity that remained stable during the pandemic, suggesting its centrality in mass responses to uncertain and novel stimuli. We then show that even before strong party cues emerged, worldview structured Americans' reactions to COVID‐19 and constrained the positions parties could take. Worldview's influence was both direct and indirect, channeled through its relationship with partisan preference. While partisanship is a potent force in political belief systems, much of its effect, we suggest, comes from its association with people's general philosophy about life.

articles.title: Identity threat, personal values, and political attitudes: Evidence from a large‐scale survey across the European Union
articles.abstract: In political contexts, identities are typically based on shared values. Populist rhetoric often utilizes real and perceived threats to evoke such identities, especially on the far right. Using dedicated items in a survey covering all 27 EU Member States ( N = 27,032), we present evidence on the understudied link between perceived identity threat and values, reflecting foundational motivations of people, as well as downstream political attitudes. At the EU level, personal values related to anxiety avoidance correlate positively with perceived identity threat, whereas growth‐focused values correlate negatively. The positive relationship between identity threat and values focusing on increasing one's self‐efficacy and status is especially pronounced, suggesting compensatory motivational processes. National‐level analysis reveals a more nuanced picture. Perceived identity threat correlates strongly with lower support for liberal policies. This result is relatively homogenous across the EU‐27 and holds when controlling for personal values. Overall, the findings resonate with populist rhetoric focusing on in‐groups and status while attacking liberal policies and universalist values. Conversely, the findings offer hope that policies and communication reducing identity threat may reinforce support for liberal policies and aligned values.

articles.title: Measuring affective polarization: Matching concepts to measures
articles.authors: James N. Druckman, Samara Klar, Yanna Krupnikov, Matthew Levendusky, John Barry Ryan
articles.abstract: Affective polarization is the extent to which partisans like their own party relative to their dislike of opposing parties. High levels of affective polarization in the United States and many other countries have prompted widespread scholarly interest and practical concern. Yet, despite nearly 15 years of scholarship, significant uncertainty remains about how best to measure affective polarization. We offer a comprehensive review focused on the measurement of affective polarization, underscoring how seemingly innocuous choices can yield substantially different results. These include the target of evaluation (e.g., engaged ideologues, ordinary voters), the dimensions of evaluation (e.g., liking/disliking, moralization), the measurement context (e.g., whether respondents are interviewed by an interviewer or complete surveys independently) and the political context (e.g., the power relationship between parties). We conclude that the next generation of inquiry will need to more carefully align measures of affective polarization with specific research questions.

articles.title: Beyond prejudice reduction: Personal and civic effects of intergroup contact among marginalized youth in Northern Ireland
articles.authors: Danielle L. Blaylock, Patrick F. Kotzur, Alexander W. O'Donnell, Rhiannon N. Turner, Stephanie Burns, Laura K. Taylor, Linda R. Tropp
articles.abstract: Intergroup contact reduces prejudice, but its potential to foster broader personal and societal change remains understudied. We address these gaps by examining a large‐scale peacebuilding intervention (PEACE4Youth) among marginalized youth in post‐conflict Northern Ireland. Using latent growth curve modeling across three waves, we demonstrate that increased intergroup contact is associated with improvements not only in youth's outgroup attitudes but also in their self‐esteem, leadership skills, and civic engagement. Youth with steeper contact gains showed the strongest growth across all domains, supporting intergroup contact as a mechanism for multidimensional change. While effects emerged across Catholic and Protestant youth, baseline differences underscore the role of pre‐existing disparities. These findings extend contact theory by empirically linking contact to personal and societal development, redefining it as a tool not only for harmony but also for empowering individuals to transform divided societies.

articles.title: How to Upend America in 100 Days: Unilateral Power at the Outset of Trump’s Second Term
articles.abstract: President Trump used the unilateral power of the presidency in extraordinary ways during the first 100 days of his second term. This article examines his use of executive action using a dataset of every action issued in the first 100 days of Trump’s second term, along with a similar dataset for his first term and other recent administrations. At the outset of his second term, Trump issued substantially more executive actions than his own first administration and his recent predecessors; however, this also came with historically low legislative productivity. His unilateral policy making is notable for the many revocations of previous executive actions and startling uses of the pardon power. The areas that Trump acted within most were government operations, tariff policies, and policies related to law and crime. These findings reveal important details of Trump’s unilateral presidency and demonstrate that his executive actions are likely to erode the traditional boundaries of presidency power if not held in check by other institutional actors.

articles.title: Predatory Journals: Do They Publish Undergraduate and AI-Generated Papers?
articles.abstract: Predatory journals are criticized widely for weak peer-review and profit-driven editorial practices, but little empirical evidence assesses their capacity to publish low-quality or AI-generated research. This study examines the level to which these journals publish undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts. We submitted papers to 144 predatory journals identified through spam solicitations, Beall’s list ( https://beallslist.net ), and the Predatory Journals database ( www.predatoryjournals.org/news/predatory-journals-list-2025 ). This included 19 undergraduate political science and human rights essays and 10 AI-generated engineering case reports to test the degree to which these essays are published. We find that most undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts are accepted, which confirms the low quality of these outlets and the risk emanating from them.

articles.title: Beyond the Greenback: Currency Power in a Greener, More Fragmented World
articles.abstract: Structural shifts in the global economy are reshaping the foundations of international currency power. This article explores how the green transition, geopolitical realignment, and sustained US protectionism could interact to transform the global currency hierarchy, with a particular focus on the US dollar and the Chinese renminbi (RMB). We highlight two key drivers of currency usage: (1) the liquidity and availability of a currency for cross-border transactions; and (2) the strategic economic and political alignment between currency issuers and their partners. Considering developments in green value chains, evolving alliances, and trade policies, the article outlines how China’s growing role in critical minerals, infrastructure finance, and alternative financial systems can enhance the internationalization of the RMB. Concurrently, US protectionism and withdrawal from multilateralism may open up space for regional currency diversification. These trends point to an increasingly fragmented and multipolar international monetary system, in which currency power will have a central role in shaping the future global order.

articles.title: The long decline of trust in democratic institutions
articles.abstract: I document declining trust in the Executive and Legislative branches of the US federal government from 1972 onwards. Data are from General Social Survey questions asking whether respondents “have a great deal”, “only some,” or “hardly any” confidence “in those running these institutions”. Net confidence (percentage difference between “great deal” and “hardly any”) in the two branches has declined continually from nearly zero in the early 1970s, accelerating substantially from the 1990s on. Different processes drive this decline for each branch. Partisan and ideological opponents of the President increasingly distrust the incumbent while supporters are roughly neutral. Trust in the US Congress has been eroding more uniformly across all parties and ideologies. In recent years net confidence has been around -30 for the Executive and -45 for Congress. This profound distrust (10 times as many have hardly any v a great deal of confidence in Congress) is widely shared across main socio-demographics, such as age, gender, income, etc., though the decline is steeper for older and white respondents. The decline is also greater than for other institutions, including until recently the third branch (Supreme Court). I close by discussing implications for research in public choice.

articles.title: Beyond free riding or free racing: a framework for understanding subnational tax policy interdependence
articles.abstract: Subnational governments operating under the same federal fiscal arrangements often make markedly different tax policy choices. Research explains this variation through vertical relationships between subnational and national governments, horizontal relationships among subnational governments, or both, and along either economic or political logics. This study offers a unifying analytical framework integrating these dimensions and logics to help scholars locate their research within the wider literature, identify adjacent processes that may interact with or confound their focal mechanisms, and specify appropriate empirical strategies. I illustrate the framework’s value through analysis of Mexico’s state vehicle ownership tax (2008–2024). Situating the analysis within the framework yields three competing arguments about how horizontal economic and political logics interact. Spatio-temporal analysis shows that partisan competition, not geographic proximity, is the primary channel of horizontal tax policy interdependence. This partisan effect is conditional on neighbors’ tax activity, but in an unexpected way: it is strongest where neighboring states hold their taxes steady and weakest where they are cutting most heavily. The case demonstrates the framework’s usefulness in revealing new substantive findings and prompting new theoretical questions.

articles.title: Allocating faculty compute budgets
Social identification and equilibrium law enforcement
articles.abstract: This paper studies how social identification reshapes the political economy of law enforcement. In a two-class economy with property crime, individuals choose whether to offend, vote over the detection probability under majority rule, and choose whether to identify with their class or with the encompassing nation. In the absence of identity concerns, class-specific material preferences over enforcement depend on victimization exposure, tax incidence, and the option value of offending. With class identification, voters place greater weight on the relative payoff of their own group, so social identity amplifies the underlying distributive conflict. With national identification, voters place greater weight on aggregate payoffs, compressing preferred enforcement levels across groups. Endogenous identity choice produces distinct political regimes and can generate multiple equilibria: societies in which class differences are more salient in identity space are more likely to sustain class identification and more extreme enforcement outcomes, whereas higher national prestige favors national identification and policies closer to the aggregate benchmark. An extension in which offending carries an action-based social deviance cost preserves the main mechanism and shows how compliance norms can reinforce class-based identity.

articles.title: War propaganda without misinformation? Normative framing and side-taking in war
articles.abstract: How do citizens of third-party states form sympathies in foreign wars? Most prior work on wartime public opinion focuses on the effects of information: material costs, elite assessments, and characteristics of combatants. Yet wartime coverage must also make choices about how to frame a conflict, separate from endorsements or facts. For example, a military intervention might be introduced in the context of one state’s sovereignty or the other state’s quest to restore democracy, even holding the facts constant. We argue that these normative frames have a large impact on public sympathy and support, especially in third-party publics, for whom material costs may be secondary considerations and loyalties may be open to debate. We demonstrate these effects with two vignette experiments among a representative sample of 1200 American adults. Framing decisions swayed respondents’ moral judgments and sympathy by 40–65 percentage points, and support for military aid by 20–30 percentage points. These effects were large and consistent regardless of the characteristics of warring parties, respondents’ foreign policy views, or their attitudes on current events such as the wars in Gaza or Ukraine.
